Top of the News

  • 14 Oct 2026

    Microsoft Releases 1,400+ Patches and “Risk Cohorts” System

    Microsoft's Patch Tuesday release for October 2026 addresses at least 1,413 vulnerabilities in its products — surpassing September's record count of 974 — including a fix for one flaw disclosed prior to its patch and one flaw known to be under active exploitation at the time of disclosure. CVE-2026-96951, CVSS score 8.8, allows an unauthorized attacker to bypass the Mark of the Web (MoTW) security feature over a network by exploiting a command injection vulnerability in Windows Shell. This flaw affects Outlook.com and versions of Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server. Microsoft notes that successful exploitation requires a targeted user to take an action to view a specially crafted malicious file. Microsoft lists the flaw as exploited, and it has been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (CISA KEV) with a three-day mitigation window for agencies bound by BOD 26-04. The SANS Internet Storm Center highlights several other notable vulnerabilities, including another security bypass caused by an untrusted search path in .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398, CVSS score 8.8); this is the flaw that was disclosed prior to the patch release. CVE-2026-70571 allows unauthorized code execution over a network due to a stack-based buffer overflow in Microsoft Exchange Server. Ten remote code execution vulnerabilities, five of them critical, were disclosed in Windows DHCP Server, and a noteworthy quantity of vulnerabilities were disclosed in Microsoft Office, emphasizing the need for prompt patching. A Microsoft blog released alongside the security updates encourages organizations to implement analytical categories called "Risk Cohorts," which group CVEs by shared "questions about deployment, exposure, trust boundaries, and usage patterns [...] that can inform prioritization," in an effort to focus the vulnerability management process.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 6

      1,400+ vulnerabilities, 76 of which are rated critical, 7 of which require no user interaction to exploit. Not such a nice way to start your day, particularly if you're bound by the KEV and need to apply the updates by October 16. At this point we've talked about grouping systems for updates according to risk — if you're still wanting to analyze CVEs but see 1,400 as a lot to analyze, the Microsoft Blog gives you an option to consider where you group updates into risk cohorts, breaking down the problem and cross cutting it according to your environment. Even so, don't get caught up in analysis paralysis: You need to have significant places where updates are applied autonomously. These numbers aren't getting smaller, and it really feels good when you check systems for updates after a bulletin like this and see they're all applied.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 6

      I've said a few times this year that "patch them all" isn't a realistic plan for the scale of vulnerabilities discovered and disclosed today. That said, I still read these mega releases as mostly good news: vendors are clearing decades of technical debt with AI-assisted testing before attackers find the same bugs. While no one really wants another standard or measurement, Microsoft's Risk Cohorts system is smart. Cohort-based vulnerability management is probably a trend we'll see emerge as best practice over the next few years. Grouping CVEs by deployment, exposure, and trust boundaries is the exposure-based prioritization vuln management teams need. I think hearing it from the vendors themselves will also help reinforce to leadership that it's not a capability problem, but a prioritization/noise/volume problem that even the vendors recognize isn't manageable with the “old ways.”

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 3 of 6

      This seems like a crazy number of patches, but consider how many of them are in the news for causing chaos and destruction: none of them. One is described as a zero-day, but is nothing to get excited about. AI is good at finding vulnerabilities, but isn't great at finding ones that really matter, and AI discovery has clearly been unleashed at the world's largest software producers. I'd argue that most of these 1,400 patches are simply software bugs, not worthy of calling 'vulnerabilities,' as they're not making anyone more vulnerable. Risk Cohorts make a lot of sense. One of the sins of vulnerability management tooling is not speaking in the language of the asset owner. Instead of "install this list of CVEs on these IP addresses," we should translate this into, "Microsoft Office is out-of-date and needs to be updated on all laptops."

      Adrian SanabriaFounder and Principal Researcher
    • Slide 4 of 6

      Adrian makes a really good point about the need to speak the language of asset owners rather than simply throwing CVE numbers at them. With more than 1,400 vulnerabilities in one Patch Tuesday, the raw numbers can become overwhelming. I'm intrigued by Microsoft's proposed risk cohorts because they encourage us to ask meaningful questions about exposure, deployment, and trust boundaries, and then apply those answers across groups of vulnerabilities. This approach has great promise as part of emerging VulnOps practices within organizations, helping teams move from vulnerability enumeration toward more intelligent, business-aware prioritization and remediation. But we need to be careful here. Even if many of these flaws turn out to be difficult to exploit in practice, we shouldn't assume they're unimportant merely because they haven't made headlines. An obscure vulnerability can become extremely important when it affects the wrong system in the wrong place. Group the analysis where it makes sense, but keep the dangerous exceptions front and center. That's a core tenet of VulnOps: the goal isn't to win at counting vulnerabilities. It's to make the right systems safer, faster.

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 5 of 6

      It’s been a bumper month for Microsoft vulnerability remediation, and AI-accelerated testing means this high volume will likely persist into the new year. To prevent attackers from reverse-engineering patches and weaponizing flaws, organizations must prioritize automated patching. Treat Risk Cohorts as optional if they fit your workflow, but make patch automation your primary defense.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 6 of 6

      I have always contended that the number of patches is an inverse measure of quality, that patching passes the cost of quality from the supplier to their customers, and that it is an inefficient way to achieve essential quality. The recent application of AI to vulnerability discovery by both rogue hackers and suppliers suggests that the quality was even worse than we suspected. Remediating that quality is all but overwhelming both the suppliers and their customers. Going forward it is to be hoped that the use of AI for discovering and eliminating vulnerabilities in the legacy code base and avoiding them in new code should improve quality. That should manifest itself in a reduction in the rate of patches.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 14 Oct 2026

    Cisco Vulnerability Exploited (CVE-2026-76519)

    On Wednesday, October 14, Cisco published a security advisory addressing a critical path traversal vulnerability in the Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature of Cisco Secure Email Gateway (CVE-2026-76519, CVSS score 9.8). The vulnerability "could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system, ... [and] is due to improper handling of email attachments when the file reputation service is enabled. ... A successful exploit could allow the attacker to write arbitrary files and execute commands with root privileges on the underlying operating system." Users are urged to update to fixed versions of Cisco AsyncOS Software for Cisco Secure Email Gateway Release: users running version 15.5 should update to version 15.5.5-014 or later; users running version 16.5 should update to version 16.5.0-780 or later; and users running version 16.0 are advised to migrate to a fixed release. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-76519 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on October 14 with a mitigation deadline of October 17 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. Cisco released four additional security advisories this week. Cisco Meraki Security Hardening Release: October 2026 addresses seven CVEs with a maximum severity of critical. Cisco Secure Email Gateway and Secure Email and Web Manager Security Hardening Release: September 2026 addresses five CVEs with a maximum severity of critical. Cisco UCS and UCS-Based Appliances UEFI Shell Secure Boot Bypass Vulnerability addresses one high-severity CVE. Finally, Cisco Advance Notification for Publication of October 21, 2026, Security Advisories notes that next week, Cisco will publish advisories addressing vulnerabilities in Expressway Series (security hardening release), IOS XR Software for ASR 9000 Series Routers, Secure Client, Snort (security hardening release), and Unified Communications products (security hardening release).

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 4

      I heard that, no, you're not going to be able to just block all attachments, nor ignore them, allowing everything through. Given the criticality of email security, even coupled with your EDR, you want to jump on this. The flaw can be exploited remotely without authentication. There are no workarounds; you gotta patch, and only after you've updated and double checked that the security configuration follows the latest guidance can you take a pause to grumble about untrusted input validation.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 4

      I recently learned from a cyber insurance provider that security gateways are associated with higher insurance claims. Not only do these have significant attack surface, but buyers rarely enable enforcement. Nobody wants to explain to executives why critical emails were quarantined or blocked — it's not worth the intra-company political risks.

      Adrian SanabriaFounder and Principal Researcher
    • Slide 3 of 4

      Oof. An email security gateway is supposed to inspect potentially dangerous attachments before they reach users. Here, processing a malicious attachment could give an unauthenticated attacker root privileges on the gateway itself. That's a particularly ugly trust-boundary failure. And consider what an attacker might do with that level of control. Beyond compromising the appliance, they could potentially manipulate, inject, or suppress messages flowing through it. A broad campaign poisoning organizational email would be bad enough. But imagine an attacker using that compromised gateway to inject carefully crafted messages targeting executives or other high-value individuals. Those messages would arrive through infrastructure the organization already trusts. That's a potentially devastating stepping stone for further attacks. These systems need rigorous patching, restricted administrative access, and monitoring from outside the appliance. Cisco specifically warns that attackers with root privileges could remove evidence of their activity. If the guard at the gate becomes the attacker, who’s watching the gate?

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 4 of 4

      While mitigation deadlines are not binding on private enterprises, they should be used in prioritizing mitigation.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 14 Oct 2026

    Ivanti Patches Actively Exploited Vulnerability in Connect Secure

    Researchers at Volexity have "identified active in-the-wild exploitation of a vulnerability chain allowing unauthenticated remote code execution in Ivanti Connect Secure VPN devices." On Tuesday, October 13, Ivanti released updates to address two of the three flaws in the exploit chain: a high-severity authentication bypass and a remote code execution vulnerability in Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2026-104935, CVSS score 8.6). These issues affect Ivanti Connect Secure versions 25.1.1.1 and earlier, 25.1.2.2 and earlier, and 22.8R2.4 and earlier. According to the Register, "the vendor said it previously identified 'a portion of this vulnerability' and patched it in July's 25.1.3.0 update, and had been working on backporting the same fix since then, however, attackers began exploiting it before that work was complete." The third flaw in the chain is a privilege escalation flaw not tracked by CVE-2026-104935; Volexity explains that “Ivanti is working on a fix for the privilege escalation vulnerability, and it will be included in a future release in the coming weeks.” The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-104935 to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) database on October 13, 2026 with a mitigation deadline of October 16 for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 4

      There’s a particularly nasty detail in Volexity’s excellent investigation: The compromised VPN appliance was fully patched at the time of the attack. The exploit chain included a mismatch between the URL used to make an access-control decision and a different path in a request header used to route the request to protected functionality. Sound familiar? We've been discussing these kinds of trust-boundary and input-interpretation problems in recent NewsBites issues. The attackers then chained additional vulnerabilities to gain root privileges, went hunting for Active Directory credentials and other sensitive information, and attempted to erase their tracks. Patch immediately, absolutely. But don't stop there. Hunt for evidence of compromise beyond the VPN appliance itself, examine external logs and forensic artifacts, and evaluate which credentials may need to be rotated. Kudos to Volexity for some outstanding forensic work.

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 2 of 4

      So we have: Privilege Escalation, Remote Code Execution, Authentication Bypass, and AD/LDAP data exfiltration, coupled with a payload which cleans up traces of their activity; read the Volexity blog for details. This is where you want off-device logs for analysis. You need to apply the updates from Ivanti (if you're not on 25.1.12+ get there), verify you've implemented the current security guidance, and quadruple check no management interface is externally reachable, while hunting for the IoCs. The fix addresses the authentication bypass and remote code execution aspects of the flaw, so keep an eye out for another update which addresses privilege escalation.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 3 of 4

      Ivanti says it identified "a portion of this vulnerability" and fixed it in July's 25.1.3.0 update, then was still backporting the fix to other branches when attackers started exploiting it. When a vendor knows a flaw exists and a backport is in progress, customers on those branches should be told so they can decide whether to upgrade, add mitigations, or start hunting. The timeline here bothers me. While I know nothing is perfect, we're operating in a threat landscape where people need more data, faster, to make decisions on risk and delays in that rollout increase risk. Balanced transparency will be an important part of the vuln management way of the future.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 4 of 4

      Vulnerabilities in VPNs and firewalls are particularly risky. Timely patching is important. However, this is a highly competitive market; there are lots of VPNs and firewalls. Consider switching to products and brands with a stronger record.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 15 Oct 2026

    Follow-up: Supermarket Refrigeration Controller Cyberattack Targeted Devices from Multiple Vendors

    The recent attack against internet-connected controllers for freezer, refrigeration, and cold storage room units in French supermarkets targeted not only AK-SC and AK-SM series devices from Danfoss, but also XWEB devices from Dixell and its parent company Copeland. The attackers manipulated the appliances' defrost mechanisms, causing them to reach temperatures of up to 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit). Ars Technica writes: "Multiple security advisories and public research reports show that all three of the controller models reportedly hacked in the incident ... contained critical vulnerabilities that allow attackers to remotely log in to the devices with the same system rights as administrators." In early August, researchers at Claroty disclosed vulnerabilities in devices from all three manufacturers: three vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM 800A controllers, which were addressed in a firmware update in August 2025, and nearly two dozen vulnerabilities in Copeland XWEB devices, which were addressed in a firmware update in February 2026. Danfoss told CoolingPost that most of the affected units were either legacy devices or devices running outdated firmware: AK-SM800 reached end-of-life in 2021, and AK-SC355 systems were discontinued in 2016; neither receives updates. CERT-FR urges the operators of the targeted devices to remove them from the internet and allow access only via secure VPN or a protected network. CERT-FR says that "simple filtering of the source IPs of refrigeration service providers on a firewall is possible, but this solution should not be considered as a long-term solution."

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 6

      Earlier this week I said exposure is rarely a decision someone approved, and the follow-up reporting backs that up. These weren't zero-days, they were old flaws and (some) end of life software. When end-of-life (EOL), unpatchable software is left internet-exposed, and no one owns the decision to retire it or wall it off, you end up with a sitting duck. I appreciate CERT-FR's pointer that source-IP filtering "should not be considered as a long-term solution," because that kind of 'quick fix' stopgap quietly becomes permanent. I always like to leave you with something actionable, so if you run facilities equipment: Find out which controllers are past end-of-life and who is accountable for them, get them off the internet and behind a VPN or protected network, and put a replacement date in the budget instead of (or at least alongside) a firewall exception.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 2 of 6

      Two things: We moved from monitoring — assuring the devices, freezers and refrigeration in this case — to controlling their behavior without modification of the access process, as well as introducing control devices needing updates, and lifecycle replacements. Call it what you would, IoT, ICS, or OT, they are all over our enterprise, large or small, and the issue is the same: you need defense in depth, coupled with lifecycle management. In other words, culture change. Be kind working with owners of these devices, they are likely working flawlessly, regardless of security, and at this point if they caught wind of this story they are wondering if they are vulnerable.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 3 of 6

      The phrase "wakeup call" is overused, but appropriate in this case, I think. This is just one example of the damage attackers could do when chaos is the only goal. We're honestly lucky there aren't more chaotic actors out there — we've been shouting about unprotected critical infrastructure exposed to the Internet for decades, even before Shodan made it painfully obvious in 2009. This constitutes a serious disruption in the food supply chain; consider smaller towns that rely on a single grocer, for example. Or the concentration risk of all the major grocery stores using the same brand equipment or supplier. The wakeup call here is for governments to realize that some agency should be getting ahead of these issues and working with operators and business owners to secure these systems before some group of teenagers or AI agents decides to spoil more food.

      Adrian SanabriaFounder and Principal Researcher
    • Slide 4 of 6

      The latest findings introduce an interesting twist to the story. The attackers reportedly compromised refrigeration controllers from multiple vendors, many of which were running outdated firmware or were no longer supported. This raises a larger concern about the growing population of industrial equipment that remains mechanically functional long after its software becomes obsolete. We need to think about cybersecurity throughout the operational life of these systems, including what happens when the manufacturer stops providing software updates.

      Marcus (Marc) SachsSenior Vice President and Chief Engineer
    • Slide 5 of 6

      This cybersecurity incident is rapidly becoming a case study in three major security pitfalls: using end-of-life hardware and software, lacking an operational technology (OT) patch management process, and failing to eliminate unnecessary internet-facing devices. Regardless of whether food distribution (i.e., supermarkets) officially qualifies as critical infrastructure, it remains a critical business risk that must be actively assessed and mitigated.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 6 of 6

      There will be a lot of essential but relatively inexpensive measures taken by the victims in the wake of this attack. Many of these were suggested by my colleagues in Tuesday's Newbites. Similar measures should be taken by others in anticipation of similar attacks and mitigation of risk.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 15 Oct 2026

    Targeted Ads Serve Mercenary Spyware Without User Interaction

    Researchers from the Citizen Lab at the University of Toronto have published a report investigating spyware campaigns that use targeted ads to deliver mercenary spyware without user interaction required. Citizen Lab calls this "the first public technical confirmation" of this attack technique, dubbed "AdFection," which uses the real-time bidding (RTB) process to push a malicious ad to a browser or app, first profiling the device and then requesting JavaScript from a command-and-control (C2) server to deploy spyware if the device is being targeted; this happens when the ad is rendered, and can occur in the background, out of user view. The researchers identified the ad buyer as Discover-Tech, a company that "presents itself as a legitimate advertising company" and is listed as an approved vendor by Google and IAB Europe, serving ads on major networks including Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. However, Discover-Tech "operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners," including Candiru, Intelos, and Bindecy. The spyware partners use Discover-Tech's "Controlium" platform to "de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered;" Citizen Lab describes a specific infection in which at least 45 devices belonging to the news media organization Al Jazeera were targeted with Candiru spyware. Analysis of nearly four billion ad bidding records publicly exposed on a Discover-Tech website showed that, between March and June 2026, "Discover-Tech ads were displayed in over 70,000 mobile apps, and over 120,000 websites." The report concludes by contending that "these security risks make it apparent that there is an urgent public-interest need to reform digital advertising," calling upon ad vendors, regulators, and lawmakers to take the problem seriously and work to stop attacks like this. Citizen Lab offers specific protection guidance for defenders and those who may be targeted, such as ad blocking methods and minimization of tracking; news organizations in particular are urged to seek expert assistance to clean and protect their systems.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 5

      The analysis from Citizen Labs largely hinges on actions for advertisers and legal/regulatory improvements to stop the behavior. For the rest of us, it's not just a case of not clicking or engaging with ads; the primary mitigation is ad blockers and opting out of targeted advertising IDs. Time to consider making these mitigations mandatory on sensitive and targeted users. Double down on lockdown mode when traveling in risky areas, remove unneeded/unsupported apps (we all have them; when's the last time you cleaned house?), and consider loaner devices issued for travel, like smart phones, tablets and laptops, which are wiped and reimaged between trips.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 5

      This is just yet another reason why ad blockers have become best practices in endpoint management. Not only are ads effectively untrusted code from an unknown source separate from the host website or application, but they've never done a good job policing the content of the ad nor the KYC of the companies bidding on ads. Finally, adtech has become the ultimate targeting tool, which was a key benefit to the attackers in this case, who were targeting journalists at Al Jazeera.

      Adrian SanabriaFounder and Principal Researcher
    • Slide 3 of 5

      Yikes. Advertisers have spent decades optimizing the online advertising ecosystem to deliver precisely the optimal content to precisely the right person at precisely the right moment, all to influence what we buy. Now attackers can turn that same machinery toward delivering spyware to precisely the right victim, without so much as a click. That's downright ominous. The technical sophistication that makes personalized advertising so profitable also makes it an extraordinarily powerful targeting mechanism for mercenary surveillance. Ad blockers can help protect individuals, but this problem cannot be solved solely by the people receiving the ads. Ad networks and exchanges that profit from this infrastructure need to exercise real due diligence in vetting their customers, scrutinizing executable content, detecting abuse, and blocking attacks from propagating through their infrastructure. And when they fail to exercise reasonable care, meaningful legal liability should reach those operating the networks, not merely the spyware vendors themselves. Reform of the digital advertising ecosystem is long overdue. Kudos to Citizen Lab for uncovering this frightening activity. The system designed to personalize our advertisements should never become the system that personalizes our compromises.

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 4 of 5

      Citizen Lab deserves credit for highlighting this overlooked malware delivery threat. Because regulators and legislators have yet to focus on the issue, ad blocking technology remains the only effective line of defense.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 5 of 5

      Vulnerabilities in browsers expose more organizations and applications than purpose-built single-application clients.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 14 Oct 2026

    Agents Deployed to Waste Scammers’ Time and Collect Information

    A startup based in Sydney, Australia is using AI agents to engage with scams via phone, email, web browser, and social media to gather fraud intelligence while taking up the scammers' time and resources. This implementation stems from university research into the use of machine learning to collect specific content from scam calls, such as "bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites," impersonated brands, and other information. These details can then be used in proactive anti-fraud measures and efforts to disrupt scam campaigns; the company's current customers include banks, utilities, telecommunications companies, and government agencies.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 4

      I love this one. It's the same automation scammers use against victims, pointed back at them. Wasting their time is fun, but the intelligence is the real value: Bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, and impersonated brands pulled from live scam conversations can provide valuable intelligence for banks and telecom providers to shut down criminal infrastructure faster. I would love to see more research on how often this kind of intel turns into disruption of the criminal activity, and how we can make it faster.

      Melissa BischopingDirector of Secure Operations and Enablement
    • Slide 2 of 4

      In other words, an AI powered honeypot (or tar pit if you prefer). You know how you call the help desk and you get their AI and it gives you the long answer to your simple question? Imagine if the scammers had to deal with that, at scale; it would definitely reduce their throughput. Now gather the interaction data centrally and develop a profile of scammers you could forward to law enforcement. Kind of cool, isn't it? Apate has $10 million in startup funding to do this, I'm keeping an eye on this, at a minimum there are going to be some fun stories as a result.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 3 of 4

      Ha! I absolutely love this idea. Scambaiters like Kitboga have been tying fraudsters in knots for years, while projects like the Jolly Roger Telephone Company and O2's AI granny Daisy have demonstrated the joy of keeping crooks occupied with conversations that go absolutely nowhere. Now imagine scaling this approach across phone calls, email, texts, social media, and beyond. Every promising victim turns out to be another defender-controlled AI agent. Every tantalizing lead draws the attacker deeper into a web of deception. Meanwhile, defenders collect attacker phone numbers, cryptocurrency wallets, malicious domains, and other intelligence useful for disrupting criminal operations and enhancing detection across our ecosystems. I would LOVE to see attackers and their automation wandering through a vast hall of mirrors, never quite sure what's real and what’s another deception. Of course, we'd need appropriate safeguards and coordination to avoid unintended consequences. But turning the economics of automation against the fraudsters themselves? Now THAT sounds like a party I'd like to attend!

      Ed SkoudisPresident
    • Slide 4 of 4

      We are quickly moving toward an era of automated attacks countered by automated defenses, with humans serving primarily as reviewers. Attackers have automated their tactics for a while, and defenders are finally taking the same approach. Until these systems are fully in place, the general rule applies: if you receive an unsolicited email, call, or text, simply don't respond.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices

  • 14 Oct 2026

    Microsoft and Health-ISAC Disrupt Chinese Criminal Marketplace Platforms

    Microsoft, Health-ISAC, and Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) have worked together to dismantle three components of "a sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace where criminals could buy accounts, hosting services and tools used to create fake websites and online identities." Those components — CoGUI, Iron Man, and YAM Store — are responsible for sending more than one billion malicious, fraudulent messages targeting consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other organizations in more than 150 countries. These messages have generated tens of millions of dollars for the criminals. CoGUI offered ready-to-use messages and websites that impersonated trusted organizations; Iron Man offered phishing-kit-as-a service; and "YAM Store is an initial access broker (IAB) that sells infrastructure using compromised or fraudulently obtained environments in providers like Microsoft and Google." Microsoft and Health-ISAC obtained a court order from United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida, which allowed them to seize domains that served as infrastructure for YAM Store, Iron Man, and CoGUI operations. "Microsoft has already disabled more than 20,000 accounts connected to YAM Store and continues to dismantle the operation by removing infrastructure hosted on its services and blocking more than 100,000 domains used for impersonation and fraud." The effort also involved support from the Japan Cybercrime Control Center (JC3), Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint, and TRM Labs.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 2

      These fake websites are pretty clever, looking legitimate without a lot of hints except that they offer unexpected pricing on hard to find items, and fail on a reputation/integrity check. Yeah, if it looks too good to be true, it is. They are collecting identity and credit card information; if you find someone who fell for it, make sure they replace any credit card/payment forms used asap.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 2

      Criminals are specializing, cooperating, and organizing. This is increasing their efficiency and the risk to the rest of us. Organized crime requires organized law enforcement.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 13 Oct 2026

    Operation Lonestar Roundup: NK Laptop Farm Disrupted, 14 People Charged

    In Texas, FBI agents searched more than 40 residences and seized 187 laptops and KVM devices associated with a laptop farm for Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) citizens pretending to be US citizens working remotely at IT jobs at US firms. According to a US Justice Department press release, "DPRK IT workers applied for and obtained remote positions by using stolen or fabricated identity documents, virtual private networks and proxy infrastructure to appear as though they were working from within the United States. They also relied on U.S.-based facilitators who received laptops from victim companies, housed and configured those devices, installed remote-access software and transferred earnings to DPRK‑controlled accounts." In a related story, the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Ohio announced the unsealing of an indictment charging a more than a dozen individuals with wire fraud conspiracy, money laundering conspiracy, conspiracy to commit identity theft, and aggravated identity theft "for their roles in an IT worker conspiracy affecting more than 70 U.S. companies." The majority of those named in the indictment are believed to be in China; two US citizens, Michael James Bostelle of Pennsylvania and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo of Texas, have been arrested. The identities of two additional defendants remain under seal. The indictment alleges that "the defendants conspired to participate in a multi-year fraudulent scheme to obtain remote IT work to generate revenue for the government of the DPRK."

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 3

      The fake remote worker scams continue, and law enforcement is working to shut them down. Complicit citizens who operate laptop farms or provide their identities are also finding themselves on the wrong side of the law. Still, you need to use diligence vetting workers, particularly those you never meet in person. Even then, validate their identity and background, and make sure the live body you do meet is the person hired. It's getting pretty easy to fake out the on-camera identity, so the old trick of meetings with cameras on is less effective, therefore (a number of you will not like this) seriously consider requiring meeting all remote workers in person at regular intervals.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 3

      Outstanding work by the men and women in blue. Organizations are clearly improving at detecting these scams and reporting them to authorities. As reports accumulate, patterns emerge that enable large-scale takedowns like the recent operation in Texas. Unfortunately, the lure of easy money often overrides common sense in humans.

      Curtis DukesExecutive Vice President for Security Best Practices
    • Slide 3 of 3

      While remote work appears to be here to stay, hiring should be face-to-face. Note that remote work reduces that essential control, management supervision. We must compensate for that with increased automated controls.

      William Hugh MurraySANS NewsBites Editorial Board

  • 15 Oct 2026

    UK Legal Aid Agency Breach Update

    A breach of the UK's Legal Aid Agency (LAA) was identified in April 2025. Several weeks after the incident was detected, LAA discovered "that the attack was more extensive than originally understood and that the criminal group behind it had accessed and exfiltrated a significant amount of personal data." The breach disrupted LAA's online services, which were not restored until December 2025. LAA's October 14, 2026 update regarding the breach details categories of affected individuals, affected dates, and the nature of the affected data. LAA notes that the "tables should not be read as meaning that every individual within a particular group had all, or any, of the information listed exfiltrated. The information exfiltrated, if any, varies between individuals." Most of the compromised data are related "to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and 16 May 2025, or to cases that were live during" that time. LAA has since identified an additional 250,000 compromised records that are from years prior to 2007: Of those, most are from the 1990s and 2000s, and just a few predate 1990. The oldest compromised data are from 1978.

    Editor's Notes

    • Slide 1 of 2

      LAA picked the wrong week to... Seriously, this is a nightmare none of us want to live. Look at the date ranges of data exfiltrated and ask yourself how much data should be online versus archived. We all remember conversations about data retention and discoverability; nobody likes to remove information. I worked with a group that had to retain HR information for 75 years post termination/separation, counter to start when the company had no pending litigation. This doesn't mean it needs to remain in the HR systems, just be retained. And we're not going back to boxes of paper. Make sure that you communicate broadly about moving data to an archive. If you decide to delete data, expect pushback as well as locally created copies, and make sure that you fully understand the use cases before reacting.

      Lee NeelyCommunity Instructor
    • Slide 2 of 2

      1978. Wow. The oldest verified record stolen here dates back almost half a century. Think about the people behind these files. Legal aid records can contain deeply personal information about some of the most difficult and vulnerable moments in people's lives. Some records absolutely must be retained for legitimate legal, historical, or operational reasons, but retention shouldn't mean leaving sensitive information indefinitely accessible in everyday systems. Inventory it, establish deliberate retention and deletion rules, segregate what must be archived, and tightly control access. Otherwise, we're accumulating decades of potential liability for people who may have had no relationship with the organization for years. Old data can cause very current harm.

      Ed SkoudisPresident

Internet Storm Center Tech Corner

SANS Internet Storm Center StormCast Friday, October 16, 2026

Panchan Crypto Mining Worm; Exploited 0-Days in Cisco Secure Email Gateway (CVE-2026-76519), Palo Alto PAN-OS (CVE-2026-0322) and Ivanti Connect Secure

Today's episode covers the Panchan crypto mining worm spreading over SSH, plus three actively exploited zero-day vulnerabilities: a root-level remote code execution flaw in Cisco Secure Email Gateway, an authenticated root RCE in Palo Alto Networks' management interface, and a chained Ivanti Connect Secure exploit documented by Volexity.

https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10140

Panchan's Mining Island [Guest Diary]

SANS.edu intern Zachary Norwood analyzes Panchan, a Golang crypto mining worm that spreads via SSH, steals SSH keys, installs a rootkit and uses Discord for command and control, using FakeNet-NG for dynamic analysis.

https://isc.sans.edu/diary/Panchans+Mining+Island+Guest+Diary/33426

Cisco Secure Email Gateway 0-Day (CVE-2026-76519)

With the reputation feature enabled, the advanced malware protection feature lets attackers write arbitrary files and execute code as root. The flaw is already exploited and there is no workaround, so patch and review Cisco's indicators of compromise.

https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-esa-afw-zqYJkjxp

Palo Alto Networks 0-Day (CVE-2026-0322)

An already exploited, authenticated remote code execution vulnerability that runs code as root. Exploitation requires an exposed management interface.

https://security.paloaltonetworks.com/CVE-2026-0322

Ivanti Connect Secure 0-Day (CVE-2026-104935)

Volexity found three chained vulnerabilities: an authentication bypass, an arbitrary file write leading to remote code execution, and a privilege escalation. Ivanti patched the first two under one CVE; the privilege escalation appears unpatched.

https://www.volexity.com/blog/2026/10/13/a-series-of-unauthenticated-events-chained-exploitation-of-ivanti-connect-secure-zero-days/

https://hub.ivanti.com/s/article/Security-Advisory-Ivanti-Connect-Secure-CVE-2026-104935?language=en_US

No Podcast on Monday, Oct. 19th.

SANS Internet Storm Center StormCast Thursday, October 15, 2026

Orphaned VBA Macros in AutoCAD DWG Files; Ledger Wallet Hardware Implants; Docker Hub Token Bug (CVE-2026-105445); curl HTTP/2 RCE

Today's episode covers hidden Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros left behind in AutoCAD drawings, Ledger hardware crypto wallets found with LTE implants that steal seed phrases, a Docker Hub account conversion flaw that exposed personal access tokens, and a curl update fixing a remote code execution bug in HTTP/2 uploads.

https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10138

Orphaned VBA Projects Inside DWG Files

Didier Stevens found AutoCAD DWG files whose VBA projects are no longer referenced but still present inside the file, likely left behind by an AutoLISP delete command, and shows a new way to extract them.

https://isc.sans.edu/diary/Orphaned+VBA+Projects+Inside+DWG+Files/33420

Ledger Crypto Wallet Supply Chain Attack: Hardware Implants

Ledger wallets sold through authorized resellers, first in Asia and recently by MediaMarkt in Europe, were found with LTE modules and SIM cards that exfiltrate the seed phrase. Reports put losses at up to $100 million.

https://www.zetter-zeroday.com/who-is-planting-backdoors-in-ledger-crypto-wallets/

Docker Hub Account Migration Bug (CVE-2026-105445)

Converting a personal Docker Hub account to an organization moved the old user's personal access tokens to a target user without confirmation, letting an attacker authenticate as that user. Docker fixed the issue and notified affected users.

https://www.docker.com/blog/docker-hub-security-advisory-cve-2026-105445/

curl Patches HTTP/2 Upload Remote Code Execution Flaw

A new curl release fixes several vulnerabilities, including remote code execution triggered when uploading a file over HTTP/2 to a malicious server. A proof of concept is available.

https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/curl-patches-http2-upload-flaw-after.html

SANS Internet Storm Center StormCast Wednesday, October 14, 2026

October 2026 Patch Tuesday: Microsoft Fixes 1,417 Vulnerabilities; Ivanti Connect Secure Exploited; Adobe ColdFusion and Commerce Critical Patches

In today's episode: Microsoft's October 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes 1,417 vulnerabilities, including an exploited Mark of the Web bypass, plus Ivanti patches an exploited Connect Secure flaw and Adobe fixes critical ColdFusion and Adobe Commerce vulnerabilities.

https://isc.sans.edu/podcastdetail/10136

October 2026 Microsoft Patch Tuesday

Microsoft patched 1,417 vulnerabilities, 76 rated critical. CVE-2026-96951, an already exploited Windows Shell security feature bypass, skips the Mark of the Web warning. CVE-2026-108398, a publicly disclosed .NET Framework flaw, bypasses application control. Also patched: 10 remote code execution flaws in Windows DHCP Server (five critical), an Exchange Server RCE triggered by a crafted email (CVE-2026-70571), and many Microsoft Office RCE vulnerabilities.

https://isc.sans.edu/diary/October+2026+Microsoft+Patch+Tuesday/33422

Ivanti October 2026 Security Update

Ivanti fixed an Ivanti Connect Secure vulnerability already exploited in limited attacks, plus two Ivanti Neurons vulnerabilities that can leak the credentials used to connect to Microsoft Intune. Patch, then rotate those Intune credentials.

https://www.ivanti.com/blog/october-2026-security-update

Adobe Patch Tuesday: ColdFusion and Adobe Commerce

Adobe fixed 110 vulnerabilities across 11 products. Adobe Commerce has critical arbitrary code execution flaws, and ColdFusion has CVSS 10.0 server-side request forgery (SSRF) and unrestricted file upload vulnerabilities. Prioritize these two products.

https://www.adobe.com/trust/security/bulletins-and-advisories.html
